lesson_title: IAM Roles: How Services Get Permissions

lesson_intro.heading: CSA L1 · IAM Roles
lesson_intro.board_text:
IAM Roles for L1
• Role ≠ user — no long-term password
• Trust policy = who can assume
• Permission policy = what they can do
• Instance profile = EC2 wearing a role

L1 skill: READ trust + permissions when a service is denied.
lesson_intro.ren_voice: Sometimes Access Denied is not a human — it is EC2 or Lambda missing a role. Today you learn to read a role: trust policy versus permission policy. At L1 you diagnose. You do not invent new trust relationships without a senior.

whiteboard_intro.board_text:
Role anatomy
• Trust policy (who) — ec2.amazonaws.com can AssumeRole
• Permissions (what) — s3:GetObject on bucket X
• Users have passwords; roles are assumed temporarily
• Wrong trust = cannot assume; wrong permissions = assumed but denied
whiteboard_intro.ren_voice: Two documents on every role. Trust answers who. Permissions answer what. A service denied can be either — L1 learns to tell which.

segments.title: Open Roles
segments.setup_voice: IAM Roles list — service identities live here.

steps.voice: Each row is a role name. Tickets often name the role on the EC2 instance profile.

segments.lesson_voice: When an instance cannot call S3, check which role is attached, then open that role — do not create a new user for the app.

check.voice: Why should an app on EC2 use a role instead of an IAM user access key on disk?
check.response_if_correct: Temporary credentials, no long-lived keys on disk, automatic rotation via the instance metadata.
check.response_if_incorrect: Think about keys sitting on a server — what is safer?

steps.voice: Trust policy: which service or account may AssumeRole.
Permission policies: same JSON shape you already read — Effect, Action, Resource.
If trust excludes EC2 but permissions allow S3 — the instance never gets credentials. If trust is fine but S3 is missing — assume works, GetObject fails.

check.voice: EC2 can assume the role but GetObject still fails. Trust or permissions?
check.response_if_correct: Permissions. Trust already worked — the gap is Action/Resource on S3.
check.response_if_incorrect: They already assumed — which document controls what happens after assume?

segments.title: Open Roles
segments.instruction_voice: Navigate to IAM Roles on your own.
segments.completion_voice: Good. That is where service principals live.

segments.title: Synthesis
segments.question: Ticket: Lambda timeout writing to DynamoDB with Access Denied. What two role documents do you open, and what does each tell you?
segments.response_if_correct: Trust — is lambda.amazonaws.com allowed to assume? Permissions — is dynamodb:PutItem (or needed action) Allowed on the table ARN?
segments.response_if_incorrect: Name the two JSON documents on a role.

session_close.ren_voice: Roles are assumed. Trust is who. Permissions are what. L1 reads both before changing anything. Next — CloudTrail, so you can prove who changed a policy.

doubt_session.ren_response_template: Cover trust vs permissions, instance profiles, and why apps should not use long-lived user keys. Defer cross-account role crafting.
doubt_session.ren_closing: Next — CloudTrail on the board: who changed what, when.
